summary:
Nahum announces a single event: the coming destruction of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian Empire. The heading calls the book "the burden against Nineveh" (1:1) — "burden" translates the Hebrew massa, a weighty pronouncement of judgment. The author is "Nahum the Elkoshite"; Elkosh's location is now unknown, and his name comes from the Hebrew word for comfort. The book looks back on the fall of Thebes, an Egyptian city Assyria itself had sacked in 663 BC (3:8), and Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, which brackets the prophecy between those dates. Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and invaded Judah; to Judah the book says, "For the wicked will never again march through you" (1:15).

Nineveh is also the city of Jonah, set about a century earlier, when it repented and was spared; Nahum declares the sentence has now arrived. Both books draw on the self-description God proclaimed at Sinai (Exodus 34:6–7). Jonah cited its mercy — "slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (Jonah 4:2) — as his reason for fleeing; Nahum opens with the same formula and completes it: "The LORD is slow to anger and great in power; the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" (1:3). Within the same poem: "The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him" (1:7).

Chapters 2–3 describe the city's fall in quick, clipped lines: "The chariots dash through the streets" (2:4); "The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses" (2:6). A taunt asks what has become of the lions' den (2:11–12); Assyria's own palace reliefs from Nineveh show the king hunting lions. Nineveh is then measured against Thebes: "Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water?" (3:8). Thebes fell anyway (3:10). Like Jonah before it (Jonah 4:11), the book ends on a question: "All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?" (3:19).
